summary.title: Functional Programming
summary.one_liner: Functional programming models computation with pure functions, avoiding mutable state and side effects, in contrast to imperative von Neumann-style languages.
takeaways: Imperative languages reflect the von Neumann architecture, where computation modifies machine state.
Functional programming is rooted in lambda calculus (1930s) and treats functions like mathematical functions.
Pure FP avoids mutation: identifiers instead of variables, expressions instead of statements, and no side effects.
Functions are deterministic and output depends only on their parameters; execution order is not guaranteed.
In OO code, keep state private and treat variables as immutable; John Backus criticised word-at-a-time imperative style.
summary.summary: This is a Speaker Deck slide deck titled Functional Programming, presented as a set of short bullet slides rather than prose. It contrasts imperative languages, which map onto von Neumann architecture and modify machine state, with functional languages rooted in lambda calculus. The slides list FP principles: no mutation, expressions instead of statements, deterministic side-effect-free functions, and telling the computer what to do rather than how. It closes with a quote from John Backus on the weaknesses of von Neumann-style programming and a practical tip to treat variables as immutable and return values based only on parameters.
